title: Bommai Kolu: A Diaspora Guide to South India's Navratri Doll Display
excerpt: From the kalasam on the top step to the marapachi couple, how Tamil, Telugu and Kannada families build the tiered doll court that anchors Navratri — and how to start one in a US or UK home.
body:
• Bommai Kolu — called Golu in Tamil Nadu, Bommala Koluvu in Telugu homes and Gombe Habba in Karnataka — is South India's Navratri tradition of displaying dolls on odd-numbered tiers.
  • The display runs from Mahalaya to Vijayadashami and tells stories: gods and epics on the top steps, weddings, markets and daily life below.
  • The marapachi wooden couple is placed first among the dolls, and families traditionally add one new doll every year.
  • A diaspora starter version needs only 3 steps, a kalasam, the marapachi pair and a handful of dolls — the visiting and sundal-sharing do the rest.

Nine nights, a court of dolls

While the north dances garba and the east celebrates Durga Puja, South Indian homes mark Navratri by building a small court. The tradition is known as Bommai Kolu in Tamil — bommai means doll, kolu a divine presence or court — as Bommala Koluvu, the court of toys, in Telugu, and Gombe Habba, the doll festival, in Kannada. Clay and wooden figurines, many made by rural artisans and passed down through families, are arranged on tiered steps called padi, always in odd numbers — three, five, seven, nine or eleven.

The arrangement is a story told in levels. The top steps belong to the divine: the goddesses Saraswati, Parvati and Lakshmi, scenes from the Ramayana, Mahabharata and the Dashavatara. Lower steps descend into human life — weddings, temple processions, musicians, farmers, market stalls, animals, and increasingly, contemporary themes a family invents for itself. Major temples such as the Meenakshi Temple in Madurai stage elaborate public golu displays each year, and The Hindu's interactive guide this Navratri walks readers through regional variations of the tradition.

The rituals inside the display

A kolu begins before the first doll. Families set up the kalasam — a pot of water and rice with betel leaves, a coin and turmeric, crowned with mango leaves and a coconut — and light a lamp to invite the goddess. The first dolls placed are the marapachi bommai, a wooden bride-and-groom pair kept on the top steps and handed down across generations. Through the nine nights, families perform daily prayers, sing devotional songs, and prepare prasadam — sundal, a seasoned legume dish, is the signature offering — for the stream of guests.

Because the social ritual is the point. Families visit each other's homes to view the displays, exchange gifts and sweets, and hear the stories behind the dolls. For children, the kolu is often their first theatre: each tier is a scene, each doll a character, and grandparents narrate.

Recreating kolu abroad

The tradition travels well, which is why it has taken root in diaspora communities in the US, Canada and Australia. A three-step display fits an apartment corner; dolls ship from Indian craft stores or arrive in grandparents' suitcases; and the visiting custom maps naturally onto a weekend open-house. Start with the kalasam and marapachi pair, add dolls as you find them — one a year, as tradition suggests — and let the steps grow with your family. Background reading: the Wikipedia entry on Golu covers the tradition's history and regional names, and Curly Tales' explainer walks through the symbolism tier by tier.

steps.detail: Kolu is arranged on an odd number of tiers — 3, 5, 7, 9 or 11. First-timers can start with 3 or 5 using a stand, stacked boxes or a bookshelf covered with cloth.
Fill a pot with water and rice, add betel leaves, a coin and turmeric, ring the mouth with mango leaves and top with a turmeric-smeared coconut. Light a lamp before placing any dolls.
The wooden bride-and-groom pair, often passed down through generations, goes on the top steps first.
Deities and sacred figures take the upper tiers; saints, wedding scenes, animals and everyday life fill the steps below.
